reference.title: Keycloak OTP policy: the settings and their defaults
reference.shortdesc: The OTP policy of a realm decides what a one-time password (OTP) looks like in it. It sets how long a code lasts, how many digits it has, and how much clock difference Keycloak forgives. In the admin console, it’s under Authentication > Policies > OTP Policy.

section.p: The defaults below are those of a new realm in Keycloak 26.8.2, read from the admin console and from the realm’s settings in the admin REST API. An independent reference, not official Keycloak documentation.

image.alt: The OTP Policy tab of a new realm, with its default values

strow.stentry: A time-based code changes every period. A counter-based code changes each time the user asks the app for one.
The algorithm the app and Keycloak use to compute a code. The three applications Keycloak names support SHA1.
The length of a code: 6 or 8.
How many periods before and after the current one Keycloak also accepts. With 1, a code of the previous or the next period works, and a code of two periods back doesn’t.
How long a time-based code lasts.
The applications that Mobile Authenticator Setup tells users to install.
Whether a code that has signed someone in can be used again before it expires.

section.title: The same settings in the admin REST API
section.p: Each setting is a field of the realm representation, at GET /admin/realms/{realm}.

section.title: Before you change a setting
section.p: A change applies only to authenticators set up after it. Each OTP credential keeps the type, the digits, the period, and the algorithm it was set up with. When I changed a realm from 6 to 8 digits, a phone set up before the change still signed in with its 6-digit codes. To move every user to the new policy, reset each user’s authenticator: Reset a user’s one-time password in Keycloak.
